title: Why we put our masters on Arweave
desc:
When a streaming platform folds, its catalog goes with it. We have watched it happen four times in ten years.

Arweave changes the deal: you pay once, and the file outlives the company, the label, and probably you. That permanence changes how you think about a discography — it stops being inventory and becomes a record, in the oldest sense of the word.

This piece walks through what actually happens when you publish on Fontainor: the manifest, the transaction, the gateway, and why a 98/2 split is not a promotional stunt but a consequence of removing the middle.
description:
When we started Fontainor, the question we heard most was: why Arweave? The short answer is that every other option we tested treats music as a lease.

Cloud buckets disappear when invoices lapse. IPFS pins vanish when the pinning service pivots. Even the big streaming platforms — the ones that feel eternal — quietly delist thousands of tracks a year. Permanence, it turns out, is not a default anywhere on the internet. It has to be engineered.

Arweave's endowment model is the only mechanism we found that pays for storage the way the music deserves: once, forever. You pay when you publish, the network holds the principal, and the interest keeps your masters readable long after all of us are gone.

That changes the psychology of publishing. A release stops being content and becomes a record — in both senses. You think harder about the mix, the artwork, the liner notes, because you know it will outlive the hype cycle. We think that pressure makes better music.

title: Liner notes are coming back
desc:
Streaming killed the liner note. There was nowhere to put it — no gatefold, no insert, just a thumbnail and a play button.

A registry that stores text as readily as audio brings the form back. An editorial entry sits next to the release, permanently, written by the person who made the record. That proximity matters.

Here is what I put in mine: who played what, where we slept, what the bus driver said at 3am outside Nkawkaw, and why track four is in 7/8.
description:
My first record came with a booklet. Lyrics, thank-yous, a blurry photo of the studio, the name of the engineer who stayed until 4am. Streaming killed that booklet, and with it a whole layer of the music.

On Fontainor, every release carries its metadata forever — and there is room for more than an ISRC code. We are seeing artists attach essays, scans of handwritten lyrics, gear lists, even the temperature of the room on the day of recording.

Why does this matter? Because context is what turns a listener into a fan. Nobody ever tattooed a lyric they found in an algorithmic playlist. They fell in love with a world, and liner notes are the door into that world.

So here is my ask: next time you publish, write the notes. Name the bassist. Thank the venue. Etch the story next to the sound. Permanence is wasted on files alone.

title: A field guide to edition pricing
desc:
Editions are the most misunderstood lever on the platform. Price low with a big edition and you optimize for reach; price high with a small one and you optimize for patronage.

Solder sold out at 150 copies because the people who wanted it were the same people who would have bought the record twice on vinyl. Know which curve you are on.

Some practical numbers from three releases, including the one that did not work.
description:
Edition pricing is the most common question artists ask when they move to Fontainor, so here is the honest field guide.

First: scarcity only means something if you enforce it, and here it is enforced by the protocol, not by a promise. When your 150 copies are gone, they are gone. That makes your first pricing decision a real one.

A rule of thumb from the first wave of registry artists: price the first release like a handshake, not a payday. Small editions (100–300) at coffee money find their collectors fast, and a sold-out badge does more for your next release than a higher margin ever will.

Second: resist the urge to go unlimited. Unlimited editions read as background music. The registry's economics reward conviction — 98% of every sale is yours, so a 200-copy edition at $8 pays like a 2,000-stream day, except it happens once and belongs to you forever.

Finally, remember that the price is metadata too. It tells the listener what you think the work is worth. Tell them the truth.
